meta.ogDescription: Really Lewis, in The Four Loves (1960). The wording has drifted slightly in circulation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1898–1963 · British literary scholar, novelist and lay theologian
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. It comes from the chapter on friendship — chapter IV — of The Four Loves, published in 1960 and developed from a set of radio talks Lewis recorded in 1958. The sentence as he wrote it begins ‘Friendship, I have said, is born at the moment…’; the version in circulation drops the aside and shifts ‘the’ to ‘that’. The thought, and the famous ‘What! You too?’, are his.

source.excerpt: Friendship, I have said, is born at the moment when one man says to another “What! You too? I thought that no one but myself…”
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section for The Four Loves (1960) carries the sentence and places it in chapter IV: en.wikiquote.org ↗.

The same section separately records Lewis’s companion sentence — ‘Friendship arises out of mere companionship when two or more of the companions discover that they have in common some insight or interest or even taste which the others do not share…’ — also from chapter IV, which is the passage this line concludes.
Wikipedia confirms The Four Loves is a 1960 book by Lewis, based on a set of radio talks from 1958: en.wikipedia.org ↗.
Lewis’s dates — born 29 November 1898, died 22 November 1963 — are from his Wikipedia biography: en.wikipedia.org ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the sentence as Wikiquote’s sourced section transcribes it. The widely circulated form drops ‘I have said’ and reads ‘at that moment’. Lewis makes the same point a few lines earlier in the chapter: ‘The typical expression of opening Friendship would be something like, “What? You too? I thought I was the only one.”’

source.rightsNote: The Four Loves was first published in 1960, so it is firmly under copyright in the United States and elsewhere; the text is quoted here as a short extract for comment and identification. This is a rights judgement about the book, not a doubt about the attribution — the line is genuinely Lewis’s.

author.heading: About C. S. Lewis
author.metaLine: 1898–1963 · British literary scholar, novelist and lay theologian
author.bio: Clive Staples Lewis held chairs in English literature at Magdalen College, Oxford and then Magdalene College, Cambridge, and wrote across an unusually wide front — medieval scholarship, science fiction, children’s books and Christian apologetics. The Four Loves belongs to the last of those, and is the most systematic thing he wrote about friendship, a subject he thought the modern world had quietly demoted.

items.why: Lewis wrote ‘Friendship, I have said, is born at the moment…’. The popular form drops the aside and reads ‘at that moment’: Wikiquote ↗.

items.scope: The shorter ‘I thought I was the only one’ ending
items.why: Also his, but a different sentence from the same chapter — ‘What? You too? I thought I was the only one.’ The two are often spliced together into a hybrid Lewis never wrote: Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Right author, right book, very slightly wrong words: Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Lewis is arguing that friendship is not the same as companionship. People thrown together by work or circumstance are companions; friendship begins at the specific moment when one of them discovers the other shares something he thought was his alone.
The reason the line travels is that it names an experience most people have had and had no word for — and it does it in four syllables of dialogue rather than a definition.
detailsBody: The Four Loves takes its four-way division from Greek — storge (affection), philia (friendship), eros and agape (charity). This sentence sits in the philia chapter.
The book grew out of radio talks Lewis recorded in 1958, which Wikipedia notes were criticised in the United States at the time for their frankness about sex.
